newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Game for a fright in S.Africa's Kruger park?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Game for a fright in S.Africa's Kruger park?.

text.p: Rhinos and lions are thriving in South Africa's biggest game park, the Kruger, but so are tamer species -- the supermarket, bungalow, petrol station and fast-food kiosk.

Some seasoned wildlife watchers now write the reserve off as no better than an animal theme park, where air-conditioned carloads of weary parents and bored children race along smooth tarred roads, forcing park rangers to man radar speed traps.
The Kruger National Park may be the size of Belgium, but nearly a million humans a year are hard to conceal in a landscape supposed to be as wild as primeval times.

Private lodges -- and an international airport -- are springing up along the park's fences. Pressures are growing in the new South Africa where tourism is booming and everything, even a lion, must pay its way.
DUMP THE CAR AND MEET THE ANIMALS
But there still is a way to escape the modern world in South Africa's top tourist attraction and get as close to the wild as adventurers do in remoter parts of Africa.
Abandon your car at the crowded rest-camps that sometimes resemble a modern suburb, and head into the bush for dawn and dusk walks with the leopards, elephants or buffalo.
It's quite safe, or so the rangers say.
"We've never lost anyone -- it would be too bad for business," says Wouter Jordaan, one of the men who take groups of eight tourists on three-day "wilderness trails".
A ranger and guard, rifles slung over their backs, lead the silent walkers through the park's scrub, grassland and dry riverbeds to sneak up unnervingly close to the animals.
The comfort of a metal cocoon, humming engine and an accelerator pedal have vanished, and you start to look at the animals through different and more deferential eyes.
WE'VE NEVER LOST A TOURIST
On a good day, hikers can lock stares with a pride of lions or sneak upwind to within a few dozen metres (yards) of a dozing hyena, bulky buffalo or a grazing white rhino.
"A buffalo looks at you as if you owe him money," wrote author Robert Ruark, and on a trek you know just what he means.
If the big game were to charge, there would be little escape. While Jordaan says he's never lost a tourist, he once had to shoot dead a buffalo that charged his group by surprise.
Luckily, such events are rare as the rangers have almost a sixth sense for the ways of the wild.

Ranger Mbongeni Thugela, whose trail in the park's south-west also takes in Bushman cave paintings, says he would prefer to walk unarmed, as without the added safety net of a gun, his respect for the animals is greater.
Wisely, most tourists think, the park authorities said no.

Hardcore thrillseekers who want to wander unaccompanied among the animals have to cross the border to selected Zimbabwean parks, but, as one South African guide wrote, "if you get chomped or stomped by the wildlife, it's your problem".
LIONS PREY ON ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS
In the Kruger, illegal Mozambican immigrants, desperate for a better life, do face such dangers as they sneak across the park into South Africa.
One couple, startled by a group of walkers, dropped their water bottles and fled without their worn-out shoes in the direction of a pride of lions. Their fate was unknown.
Lions ate a mother and child in January who were separated from nine companions by an elephant. Soldiers, who patrol the park by bike, found their scant remains.
On some days, the big game stay out of view of trailists, but there are plenty of smaller consolations in the bush, down to the spiders, termites, animal tracks and fascinating dung.

Dung analysis is one of a ranger's many skills. If it's white it comes from a predator who has chewed up bones. If it's dark and steamy, it may belong to a rhino or elephant nearby. How the grass or leaves were chewed sheds further light.
BACK TO CAMP FOR BRUNCH AND A SNOOZE
After a few hours in the subtropical heat, the group returns to the camp from which the dawn and dusk walks begin, secluded in a part of the park barred to motorised tourists.
Only groups of rangers are allowed to camp out rough.
At night the padding of passing lions and the howls of jackals and hyaenas can be heard by the water hole, just outside a worryingly flimsy perimeter fence.

The Kruger was once reserved for white South Africans, used to being waited on by servants, and the camp, though modest with an outhouse toilet and paraffin lamps for light, is a discrete oasis of comfort in the wilderness.
To help you rise in the dark before four, an attendant brings a basin of hot water to your wooden hut.
Fresh towels are waiting, the coffee is already boiling on the camp fire and later the resident cook will get to work on brunch, after the walk and before the siesta.

For most black South Africans, a safari in the park is still too costly an affair, although three days walking trails, at 935 rand ($210) all in, cost far less than one night's stay in many of the country's upmarket private reserves.
